clinical-axsm-2019.voice: Their depression drug just hit the main target in its second pivotal trial, and the FDA already gave it breakthrough status. They say that's enough to file next year. I think this is their moment.

claims.text: second positive well-controlled trial in MDD
breakthrough therapy designation already granted
the company says the package supports an NDA filing in the second half of 2020

clinical-axsm-2019.question: Is a second positive readout enough to buy at today's price, with cash for about four quarters and four more readouts due?

debrief_check.s1: True as stated, and the pattern did not simply repeat: within the year AXS-05 met its endpoint in Alzheimer's agitation but missed against an active comparator in treatment-resistant depression [e3][e5].
debrief_check.s2: True. Designation did not shorten the road: the NDA was accepted with priority review in April 2021, then hit a deficiency letter over manufacturing and analytical methods and missed its target date, before approval as Auvelity in August 2022 [e7][e8][e9][e10].
debrief_check.s3: The company did not file within the year; the filing came about a year later than the friend's 'next year'. It also sold $174 million of stock three days after the cutoff, which answered the cash question the packet had flagged, at the cost of dilution [e1].

clinical-axsm-2019.ask_label: What would you ask your friend?

ask_friend.q: How strong was the trial?
ask_friend.a: GEMINI was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled US trial of 327 adults with moderate to severe depression [c2]. The drug beat placebo on the primary depression score at week six, 16.6 versus 11.9 points, p=0.002, with separation from week one and remission in 39.5% versus 17.3% [c1][c3][c4]. Side effects were dizziness, nausea and headache; one serious event was judged unrelated [c5]. The company says GEMINI plus the earlier ASCEND study supports a filing in the second half of 2020 [c6]; the regulator has not said so.

ask_friend.q: What else is due, and can they pay for it?
ask_friend.a: Four more readouts inside the next two quarters: the same drug in treatment-resistant depression and in Alzheimer's agitation, and a migraine drug in two trials [c7][c8]. Cash was $43.6 million at 30 September, down from $53.8 million three months earlier, with about $10.6 million used in the quarter; at that rate the packet's own scenario gives roughly four and a half quarters [c9][c11b][c11c]. Management says cash lasts into the second quarter of 2021. The company has also proposed a mid-trial design change in the Alzheimer's study that the regulator had not yet agreed [c12].

ask_friend.q: How much is already in the price?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $79.80, a 12-month high, up more than 2,500% over twelve months. Market capitalisation is about $2.75 billion with net cash of about $24 million [c11a]; there is no revenue and no approved product, so revenue multiples do not apply. The price is paying for approval and a launch that have not happened, and for a company that will need to raise money before either.

assumptions.text: The regulator will accept two trials as enough to approve the drug.
The other four readouts will go the same way as this one.
The company can raise the cash it needs without wrecking the price.
After a 25x run the price already assumes approval; the risk is down.
I don't have enough evidence to take a position either way.

thesis_check.a1: Evidence: the filing came in early 2021, later than the guided second half of 2020; the regulator accepted it with priority review, then sent a deficiency letter over manufacturing and analytical questions, missed its target date, and approved the drug in August 2022 [e7][e8][e9][e10]. For this assumption: right in the end, and outside a one-year horizon. Unknown: how much of the delay a reader could have priced in 2019; the packet did not name manufacturing risk.
thesis_check.a2: Evidence: the migraine drug won both its trials and the depression drug won in Alzheimer's agitation, but missed against an active comparator in treatment-resistant depression in March 2020 [e2][e3][e4][e5]. For this assumption: three of four, and the miss came in the same drug. Unknown: which readouts the market weighted most; the record does not attribute moves.
thesis_check.a3: Evidence: the company sold $174 million of stock three days after the cutoff [e1]. For this assumption: supported; the funding question was answered within the week, at the cost of dilution. Unknown: the price paid by earlier holders is in the result tiles, not in the record of events.
thesis_check.a4: Evidence: within the year came a big equity raise, one failed trial, three successful ones and a pandemic [e1][e3][e4][e5][e6]; see the result tiles for what the price did over your horizon. For this assumption: the price did not fall apart, nor did it run further inside the year. Unknown: the drug's later approval and launch lie beyond one year [e10][e11].
thesis_check.a5: Evidence: a year of mixed readouts and a raise, with the decisive regulatory events two years away [e1][e3][e7]. For this assumption: fair; the packet listed the catalysts but could not rank them. Unknown: whether waiting for the filing would have been cheaper; the tiles say.

walkthrough.stage_text: Three days in, the company sells $174 million of new stock. The runway question in the packet is answered; existing holders own less of the company.

Three months in, the same drug misses its primary endpoint at week six against an active comparator in treatment-resistant depression. The migraine drug won its first trial in December. Two more readouts are due within weeks.

Four months in, the drug meets its primary endpoint in Alzheimer's agitation and the migraine drug wins its second trial. Three of four readouts have gone the company's way; the filing in depression is still ahead, and a pandemic has begun.

Twenty months in, after the filing was accepted with priority review, the company discloses a regulator's letter citing deficiencies in the application. What the deficiencies are is not public; the decision date is two weeks away.

clinical-mdgl-2018.voice: Their liver-disease drug cut liver fat in a placebo-controlled trial and the biopsies show the disease actually resolving. They just raised close to half a billion, and the plenary slot at the big liver meeting says the field is paying attention.

claims.text: placebo-controlled Phase 2 met its primary endpoint on liver fat
36-week biopsies showed NASH resolution and fibrosis improvement
cash and investments of about $488 million after a June stock sale

clinical-mdgl-2018.question: Is a strong Phase 2 in a small trial, with the pivotal design still pending regulatory agreement, worth today's price?

debrief_check.s1: The regulator agreed and the pivotal trial launched in March 2019; it met both co-primary endpoints in December 2022 [e1][e5].
debrief_check.s2: Replicated in Phase 3. Breakthrough designation followed in April 2023, the NDA was accepted with priority review in September 2023, and the approval decision fell four months after this five-year window [e6][e7][e8].
debrief_check.s3: Enough to get there, with another $500 million stock sale in September 2023 to fund the launch [e9]. Compare with the five-year return in the tiles: the science the friend described was right, and the price at the cutoff had already paid for most of it.

clinical-mdgl-2018.ask_label: What would you ask your friend?

ask_friend.q: How good is the trial?
ask_friend.a: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 of 125 patients [c13]. Liver fat fell 36% at week 12 against placebo, p<0.0001, and 37% versus 8.9% at week 36 [c14][c15]. On biopsy, NASH resolved in 27% of treated patients against 6.5% on placebo, p=0.02, and fibrosis improved in half of those [c3][c16]. Side effects were mild and balanced [c18]. The caveats: biopsy endpoints are secondary, the placebo arm with paired biopsies was small, and the pivotal-trial design is still pending agreement with the regulator [c12].

ask_friend.q: Can they fund a Phase 3?
ask_friend.a: Cash and investments were $488.5 million at 30 September, up from $191.5 million, after a June stock sale that raised about $283 million [c4][c8]. Shares outstanding rose from 14.2 million to 15.4 million [c9]. Revenue is zero [c5]. At the recent operating outflow of about $6.4 million a quarter the runway looks very long, but that rate predates a 900-patient Phase 3, which management says it plans to start in late 2018 or early 2019 and believes it can fund [c6][c7][c11].

ask_friend.q: How much is already in the price?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $186.51, up more than 300% over twelve months but 41% below the 12-month high. Market capitalisation is about $2.9 billion with about $482 million of net cash [c10]; no revenue, so no multiple. A second programme in an inherited cholesterol disorder has a completed Phase 2 and no Phase 3 plan yet [c19][c20]. The price is paying for a Phase 3 that has not started in a disease where Phase 2 signals have often failed to replicate.

assumptions.text: The Phase 2 biopsy results will replicate in a large Phase 3.
The regulator will agree a trial design that this drug can pass.

I don't have enough evidence to take a position either way.

clinical-nktr-2018.voice: A major pharma has agreed to put $1 billion into a partnership with them and to buy $850 million of their stock at a premium. They're backing this cancer treatment while it's still in early trials. That makes me interested. What do you think?

claims.text: a $1 billion cash payment plus an $850 million equity purchase at a premium, agreed and pending closing
the candidate is still in early trials: a 38-patient uncontrolled dose-escalation study
the friend's inference: a big partner's backing makes it interesting (not a reported fact)

clinical-nktr-2018.question: Does a partner's cheque validate the science, or only buy an option on it? The data behind the deal comes from 38 patients in an uncontrolled study.

debrief_check.s1: The agreement closed on 3 April 2018 after antitrust clearance, and the cash and equity proceeds were received as agreed [e1].
debrief_check.s2: Early it was. As the melanoma and kidney cohorts grew past the first handful of patients in June 2018, response rates were roughly half the initial figures; twelve-month data in 2019 showed them recovering; the first randomised Phase 3, 783 patients, missed both co-primary endpoints in March 2022 [e2][e5][e7].
debrief_check.s3: The partner did commit the money and stayed in the programme for four years [e1][e6][e8]. What the backing could not tell anyone in February 2018 was whether the drug worked; the record says it did not, and that took a Phase 3 to establish.

ask_friend.q: What did the partner actually buy?
ask_friend.a: Rights to co-develop the lead candidate with its own approved checkpoint inhibitor across a joint plan of more than 20 indications in 9 tumour types. The company keeps worldwide sales and pricing authority for the candidate, and the partner pays most of the cost of the combination trials [c1][c2][c11][c12]. The upfront was $1.0 billion in cash plus $850 million of stock bought at $102.60, about a 30% premium to the prior 20-day average [c1]. The transaction was still subject to antitrust clearance and expected to close in the second quarter [c2b].

ask_friend.q: How many patients support those results?
ask_friend.a: Thirty-eight, in an open-label dose-escalation study with no control arm. The headline response rates come from sub-groups of ten or eleven: 7 of 11 in untreated melanoma, 6 of 10 in untreated kidney cancer [c3]. The dose chosen for further trials was set from this same study [c4]. Biomarker changes in blood and tumour tissue are supportive but are not outcomes [c5].

ask_friend.q: How much success is already in the stock price?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $84, up about 528% over twelve months and 95% over three. On the latest share count that is a market capitalisation near $13 billion for a company whose 2016 revenue was $165 million, and whose most recent quarter's revenue was mostly a one-time licence payment from an unrelated deal [c6][d3]. Net cash after debt was about $159 million at September 30 [d2]. There is no approved product from the lead candidate; the price is paying for the option the partner just bought.

assumptions.text: The early clinical results will hold up as more patients are treated.
The partnership removes the financing risk for years.
The current valuation still leaves enough upside if the drug works.
I don't have enough evidence to take a position either way.
The price already assumes success; the risk is to the downside.

thesis_check.a1: Evidence: response rates fell by roughly half as cohorts grew (June 2018), recovered in twelve-month data (2019), and the first randomised Phase 3 missed both co-primary endpoints (March 2022) [e2][e5][e7]. For this assumption: not supported over the full record; within the first year the evidence had already weakened it. Unknown: whether a different dose or population would have fared better; the programme ended before that was tested.
thesis_check.a2: Evidence: the $1 billion and the $850 million equity were received in April 2018, the partner stayed until April 2022, and a further financing of up to $150 million was agreed in 2021 [e1][e6][e8]. For this assumption: supported; no financing crisis appears in the record. Unknown: how much of the $150 million was drawn, and what the company's cash position was at each date, which this record does not collect.
thesis_check.a3: Evidence: the stock fell sharply within months of the cutoff and the drug later failed; see the result tiles for the return over the horizon you chose [e2][e3][e7]. For this assumption: it was never put to the test, because the condition 'if the drug works' did not occur. Unknown: what the upside would have been on success; a failed drug does not show that the earlier price already assumed success.
thesis_check.a4: Evidence: the packet itself said the data came from 38 uncontrolled patients, and the decisive Phase 3 read out four years after the cutoff [e7]. For this assumption: consistent with how the record unfolded; nothing decisive arrived for years. Unknown: a wait can also miss a winner; this record happens not to be one.
thesis_check.a5: Evidence: no event in the record added to the story the price told in February 2018; the expanded data, the short report, the litigation and the Phase 3 each subtracted from it, with the 2019 recovery as the exception [e2][e3][e4][e5][e7]. For this assumption: broadly supported, with that exception. Unknown: how much of the decline was the drug and how much the wider biotech market; this record does not separate them.

growth-007.voice: Solar manufacturer guides 2022 earnings to as little as zero after earning $4.38 a share in 2021; plans to double capital spending on new US and India plants.

claims.text: 2022 EPS guided to $0.00 to $0.60 versus $4.38 earned in 2021
2022 capex of $850 million to $1.1 billion, about double 2021
17.5 GW of 2021 net bookings and a guided $1.1 to 1.35 billion year-end net cash

growth-007.question: Is a 90% guided profit drop a temporary squeeze while capacity is built, or a margin problem the bookings can't fix?

debrief_check.s1: Worse than the headline: full-year 2022 came in at a $0.41 loss per share, below even the $0.00 low end, with $73 million of plant start-up cost. Then 2023 guidance called for $7 to $8 [e1][e7].
debrief_check.s2: Happened on schedule: the third Ohio plant started in the first half of 2023 and the India plant about a quarter late. After the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022 the company announced roughly $2.3 billion more US capacity [e2][e3][e5][e8][e9].
debrief_check.s3: The bookings and cash cushion were real, but the year's re-rating came from a law passed five months after the cutoff, which the packet flagged only as 'pending, not yet enacted'. The bull case was right for a reason it did not contain.

growth-007.ask_label: What would you look up before deciding?

ask_friend.q: Why is next year's profit guided so low?
ask_friend.a: Guidance for 2022 is net sales of $2.4 to 2.6 billion, gross profit of $155 to 215 million and diluted EPS of $0.00 to 0.60, after $4.38 earned in 2021 [c6][c4]. The company's own explanation inside the release: $10 to 15 million of underutilisation losses tied to the capacity transition, freight and input costs, and a smaller sales volume while new plants are built [c6]. What the release does not contain is any guidance beyond 2022.

ask_friend.q: Is demand the problem?
ask_friend.a: Not on the order book. 2021 net bookings were 17.5 GW-DC, 11.8 GW-DC of them since the third-quarter call, which is more than two years of the guided 2022 shipments [c7]. The plan is to double capacity: a third US plant for the first half of 2023 and a first Indian plant for the second half, with 2022 capex of $850 million to 1.1 billion, roughly double 2021 [c10][c6]. The United States was 84% of 2021 sales [c11]; India has just imposed 40% module tariffs [c12].

ask_friend.q: What is the stock already pricing?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $75.62, down 38% from the 12-month high and down 27% over three months. Market capitalisation is about $8.0 billion, or $6.5 billion after $1.6 billion of net cash, which is roughly 2.2 times 2021 revenue [c2]. The company guides to $1.1 to 1.35 billion of net cash at the end of 2022 even with the capex step-up [c6]. Note the company was loss-making as recently as 2019 [c15], and a US domestic-manufacturing incentive exists only as proposed legislation [c16].

assumptions.text: The profit drop is a one-year cost of building capacity, not a margin problem.
The order book means demand will fill the new plants.
The proposed US manufacturing incentives will become law.
After a 38% fall the price already reflects the guidance cut.
Module pricing is under structural pressure and the cut will not be the last.

thesis_check.a1: Evidence: 2022 ended in a $0.41 loss per share, below even the guided low end, with $73 million of plant start-up cost; 2023 guidance then called for $7 to 8 of EPS [e1][e7]. For this assumption: supported in direction, though the one bad year was worse than guided. Unknown: how much of the 2023 rebound came from the company's own execution versus the new tax credit.
thesis_check.a2: Evidence: both plants started on or near schedule and the company announced roughly $2.3 billion more US capacity within the year [e3][e5][e8][e9]. For this assumption: supported; demand was never the constraint in the record. Unknown: how much of the later order book depended on the 2022 law rather than the 2021 bookings.
thesis_check.a3: Evidence: the Inflation Reduction Act was signed in August 2022, five months after the cutoff, with a production credit for US-made modules [e2]. For this assumption: it happened. Three years on, the same credits became the main risk when a phase-out was proposed and then partly preserved [e10][e11]. Unknown at the cutoff: timing, which no packet could give.
thesis_check.a4: Evidence: within the year the shares roughly tripled; see the result tiles [e1][e2][e3]. For this assumption: the price at the cutoff did not reflect the guidance cut so much as ignore what came next; whether it was cheap depended on a law, not on the cut. Unknown: what the stock would have done without the Act.
thesis_check.a5: Evidence: 2022 was indeed worse than guided [e7], but 2023 guidance rebounded sharply and the US tariff circumvention finding and the tax credit changed the pricing environment [e6][e2]. For this assumption: not supported over the year; the pressure was real but was overtaken by policy. Unknown: the counterfactual without those policy changes.

walkthrough.stage_text: Two months in, the first quarter of 2022 is a loss of $0.41 a share on $367 million of sales. Guidance for the year is reiterated, not cut again. The new plants are not yet producing; the old ones are running below capacity while the transition happens.

Five months after the cutoff, the legislation that the packet listed only as proposed becomes law: a production credit per watt for modules made in the United States. The company has not yet said what it will do with it; that announcement comes two weeks later.

At the one-year mark the full-year 2022 result is a $0.41 loss per share, below even the $0.00 low end guided a year earlier, with $73 million of start-up cost. In the same release, 2023 guidance is $7 to 8 of EPS and the third US plant is weeks from production.

Three years on, a Senate committee proposes accelerating the phase-out of the same manufacturing credits the expansion was built on. Whether it becomes law is not yet known at this date; the answer came three weeks later.

baseline.narrative: Your window ends before the first new development in this record. The starting guidance cut and expansion plan are not yet enough to show why profits fell or whether the new capacity will find demand.

checks.a1: Unresolved. The starting guidance alone cannot establish whether the loss is a one-year buildout cost or a more lasting margin problem.
checks.a2: Unresolved. A reported order book at the cutoff does not establish that demand will still be there once the new plants are running.
checks.a3: Unresolved. The manufacturing incentive was only proposed at the cutoff; this record cannot establish whether or when it will become law.
checks.a4: Unresolved. No share-price outcome is available at the cutoff to establish how much of the guidance cut the price already reflected.
checks.a5: Unresolved. This record does not establish whether the pricing pressure behind the cut is structural or a one-year squeeze.

updates.narrative: The first quarter's loss tracked the range already guided, and the company left its full-year outlook unchanged rather than cutting it again.

checks.a1: Partly supported. The first-quarter loss matched guidance already issued, which the company reiterated rather than cut further. One quarter does not distinguish a temporary buildout cost from a lasting margin problem.

updates.narrative: Five months after the cutoff, the incentive law the packet had flagged only as proposed was signed, creating a new production credit for US-made solar components.

checks.a3: Supported. The manufacturing incentive legislation was signed into law, creating a per-component production credit for US-made modules. This record does not establish how durable that credit will prove.
checks.a4: Unresolved. The incentive that reshaped the outlook was legislation passed after the cutoff, not information already available when the price was set. This record does not show how much of the guidance cut itself the entry price already reflected.

updates.narrative: In the three months after the new law, the company announced roughly $2.3 billion of further US capacity across two more facilities, citing the incentive directly and continuing the buildout begun before the cutoff.

checks.a2: Partly supported. The company committed to further US capacity, including a fourth facility, citing the new law, a sign management still expected demand to fill plants under construction. New commitments do not by themselves prove the order book was sufficient.

updates.narrative: In December, regulators found that competitors were routing Chinese-made panels through other Southeast Asian countries to avoid existing duties, though a waiver meant no immediate cash impact.

checks.a5: Partly supported. Regulators found competitors circumventing existing China duties through other countries, evidence the module-pricing environment stayed contested. A duty waiver until mid-2024 means this record does not show any near-term effect on prices.

updates.narrative: At the one-year mark, the full-year loss came in worse than even the guided low end, but the company guided 2023 to a sharp rebound to $7-8 of EPS.

checks.a1: Mixed. The full-year loss was worse than even the guided low end, with $73 million of start-up cost cited, but 2023 guidance points to $7-8 of EPS. This does not settle how much of the rebound reflects execution versus the new tax credit.
checks.a5: Not supported over the year. 2022 results were worse than guided despite real pricing pressure, but 2023 guidance rebounded sharply after the new law. This record does not show whether pricing pressure eased or was simply outweighed by policy.

updates.narrative: Over the following year, both new plants named in the packet's catalysts began production: the third US facility on the guided first-half-2023 schedule, the India facility several months behind its guided second-half-2023 target.

checks.a2: Supported. Both new plants in the packet's catalysts list began production, one on schedule and one several months late. This confirms the buildout was completed as planned; it does not show whether shipments matched the new capacity.

updates.narrative: By mid-2025, a Senate committee proposed accelerating the phase-out of the same manufacturing credits the expansion had relied on, and shares fell sharply on the news.

checks.a3: Unresolved. A Senate committee proposed accelerating the manufacturing credit's phase-out from 2032 to 2028, three years after the credit took effect, putting its durability in question. Whether the proposal becomes law is not yet known at this date.

updates.narrative: The bill that followed preserved the original phase-out schedule for solar manufacturing credits, unlike wind, while adding new foreign-sourcing rules manufacturers must meet to keep claiming them.

checks.a3: Partly supported. The signed law kept the original phase-out timeline for solar manufacturing credits intact, unlike wind, but added foreign-sourcing thresholds rising to 85% by 2030. This record does not establish whether First Solar's supply chain will meet those thresholds.

clinical-srpt-2021.voice: Gene therapy for muscular dystrophy misses its main functional goal in first placebo-controlled trial; company points to protein expression and a younger-patient subgroup.

claims.text: primary functional endpoint not significant (p=0.37)
primary biological endpoint met (p<0.0001) and the 4-5 year subgroup significant
two approved drugs generate $121 million a quarter and cash is about $1.8 billion

clinical-srpt-2021.question: Is a mixed readout with a revenue base a setback to buy, or the first sign the lead program does not work?

debrief_check.s1: The miss was real and it repeated: the larger confirmatory trial also missed the same functional endpoint in October 2023, while meeting secondaries [e6].
debrief_check.s2: The subgroup carried the day with the regulator: accelerated approval for ages 4 to 5 in June 2023, expanded to all ages in 2024, then narrowed back after two liver-failure deaths and a boxed warning in 2025 [e5][e7][e8][e9][e11].
debrief_check.s3: The revenue base held and a third exon-skipping drug was approved on its deadline in February 2021; the company financed the gap with $1.13 billion of convertible notes rather than equity [e1][e4]. The packet's own 'short' column had named liver-enzyme elevation as a risk; it recurred at a fatal scale years later.

clinical-srpt-2021.ask_label: What would you look up before deciding?

ask_friend.q: What exactly did the trial show?
ask_friend.a: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 41 boys aged 4 to 7 [c1]. The gene therapy met its biological endpoint, 28.1% micro-dystrophin expression, p<0.0001, but the 48-week motor-function score was not significant against placebo [c2][c3]. In the pre-specified 4 to 5 year-old subgroup of 16 the difference was significant [c4]. Management says an imbalance between arms may have contributed [c7]. About 85% of treated boys had a treatment-related adverse event; three serious events included muscle breakdown and liver-enzyme elevation [c6].

ask_friend.q: What does the company earn meanwhile?
ask_friend.a: Two approved exon-skipping drugs produced $121.4 million of product revenue in the third quarter, up about 23%, and $380.8 million in 2019 [c11][c16][d4]. A third drug in the same class is under priority review with a decision due 25 February 2021 [c14][c15]. Cash and investments were about $1.8 billion at 30 September [c12], against a third-quarter operating outflow of about $238 million and R&D of $190 million a quarter [d2][c13]. A large pharmaceutical partner holds ex-US rights to the gene therapy under a December 2019 deal [c18].

ask_friend.q: Is it expensive?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $168.95, up 30% over twelve months and 5% below the 12-month high, before the market has traded on this readout. Market capitalisation is about $13.3 billion; net cash about $1.4 billion; enterprise value roughly 31 times 2019 revenue [c16]. That multiple only makes sense if the gene therapy reaches the market; the two approved drugs alone do not carry it.

assumptions.text: The younger-patient subgroup result is real and will convince the regulator.
The functional miss means the therapy does not work; the market is right to sell.
The revenue base and cash make this a setback, not an existential event.
The safety findings will matter more than efficacy in the end.
I don't have enough evidence to take a position either way.

thesis_check.a1: Evidence: accelerated approval for ages 4 to 5 came in June 2023, then expansion to all ages in 2024, while the larger confirmatory trial again missed the same functional endpoint in October 2023 [e5][e6][e7]. For this assumption: right about the regulator, unproven about the biology. Unknown: what the functional benefit is; two trials have not shown it in the full population.
thesis_check.a2: Evidence: the therapy reached the market on a surrogate endpoint and expanded, before deaths and a boxed warning narrowed it again in 2025 [e5][e7][e8][e11]. For this assumption: the miss did not stop approval within three years; whether it 'works' is still contested at five. Unknown: long-term function in treated boys.
thesis_check.a3: Evidence: the third drug was approved on its deadline, revenue kept coming, and the company financed itself with $1.13 billion of convertible notes rather than equity [e1][e4]. For this assumption: supported through the three-year horizon. Unknown: the 2025 safety crisis, which suspended revenue guidance [e9].
thesis_check.a4: Evidence: the packet's three serious events included liver-enzyme elevation; in 2025 two patients died of acute liver failure, shipments were paused and a boxed warning was added [e8][e9][e10][e11]. For this assumption: not visible inside three years, decisive at five. Unknown: whether the signal in 41 patients was readable as the later risk; the record only shows the recurrence.
thesis_check.a5: Evidence: a mixed readout became an approval, then a confirmatory miss, then a safety reversal [e5][e6][e8]. For this assumption: fair; each stop reversed the previous one. Unknown: any horizon shorter than five years tells a different story than the full one.

walkthrough.stage_text: Seven weeks in, the regulator approves the third exon-skipping drug on its deadline. The base business is intact; the gene therapy question is untouched.

Twenty months in, the company raises $1.13 billion in convertible notes rather than selling stock, with interest rates rising fast. Expression and safety data from the commercial manufacturing process were reported the previous year with no new safety signals.

Two and a half years in, the regulator grants accelerated approval of the gene therapy for ambulatory boys aged 4 to 5, the subgroup from the trial in the packet. A confirmatory trial is still running; its result is due in months.

Just before the three-year mark, the confirmatory trial misses its primary functional endpoint while meeting key secondary endpoints, the same pattern as the trial in the packet, now in a larger population. The approval stands for the moment.
Four years in, the company discloses the first patient death linked to the therapy, from acute liver failure. The indication had been widened to all ages the previous summer.

baseline.narrative: Your window ends before the third exon-skipping drug's approval decision or any gene-therapy trial follow-up. The starting record leaves both the subgroup finding and the funding question unresolved.

checks.a1: Unresolved. The favorable subgroup result comes from one pre-specified cut of a 41-patient trial that did not reach significance in the full population; the starting record cannot establish whether it is reproducible or how the regulator will read it.
checks.a2: Unresolved. One controlled trial's non-significant primary endpoint, with the company citing an arm imbalance not independently confirmed, is not enough on its own to establish that the therapy does not work.
checks.a3: Unresolved. Revenue was growing but the third quarter alone was a $238 million cash outflow; the starting record cannot establish whether revenue and cash will cover the gene-therapy program without further financing.
checks.a4: Unresolved. Three of 41 treated patients had serious adverse events, including liver-enzyme elevation, in a therapy intended for children; the starting record cannot establish whether safety or efficacy will prove decisive.
checks.a5: Unresolved. The starting record contains a mixed clinical readout, approved sibling drugs on a surrogate endpoint, and an unresolved financing question, with no way yet to weigh them against each other.

updates.narrative: The regulator approved the third exon-skipping drug on its guided deadline, and early data using the planned commercial manufacturing process showed no new safety signals, though one of eleven participants again had elevated liver enzymes.

checks.a3: Partly supported. The FDA approved the third exon-skipping drug, AMONDYS 45, on its guided deadline, adding to the revenue base independent of the gene-therapy program. This does not establish that revenue and cash will cover future financing needs.
checks.a4: Unresolved. Early data using the commercial manufacturing process reported no new safety signals, but one of eleven participants again had elevated liver enzymes, echoing the earlier signal. Too few patients to show whether safety will prove decisive.

updates.narrative: The company issued $1.13 billion of convertible notes due 2027. About $736 million of the proceeds repaid earlier convertible notes and term loans, so the new money added was well below the headline amount.

checks.a3: Partly supported. The company issued $1.13 billion of convertible notes and used about $736 million to repay earlier notes and term loans; the rest added to cash. Access to debt markets does not show the business can carry that debt or fund development from revenue.

updates.narrative: The FDA granted accelerated approval for ambulatory patients aged 4 to 5, on the basis of micro-dystrophin expression, a surrogate measure, with the larger confirmatory trial still pending.

checks.a1: Partly supported. The FDA granted accelerated approval for ambulatory patients aged 4 to 5, but on micro-dystrophin expression, a surrogate, not on the subgroup's functional result. Whether that functional result is real awaits the confirmatory trial.

updates.narrative: The larger confirmatory trial again missed its primary functional endpoint while meeting key secondary endpoints, repeating the pattern from the packet's trial in a bigger population; the approval stood.

checks.a1: Weakened. The confirmatory trial, run in a wider age group, again missed its primary functional endpoint, repeating the earlier pattern. Secondary endpoints favored treatment, so this does not settle whether the subgroup effect is real.
checks.a2: Mixed. The primary functional endpoint missed significance again, echoing the earlier trial, but key secondary endpoints favored treatment and the approval was not withdrawn. This does not establish either that the therapy works or that it does not.

updates.narrative: The FDA expanded approval to all patients aged 4 and older, granting traditional, not just accelerated, approval for ambulatory patients based on the totality of the data.

checks.a1: Supported so far. The FDA granted traditional approval for ambulatory patients aged 4 and up, moving beyond the accelerated, subgroup-only approval. This reflects the regulator's read of the totality of data, not independent proof of the functional effect.
checks.a2: Weakened. The regulator granted full traditional approval for ambulatory patients despite the earlier functional misses, judging the totality of the data favorably. This does not establish that the therapy works in every patient it was later given to.

updates.narrative: Two patients died of acute liver failure after treatment in the months that followed, leading the company to halt trial dosing and suspend its 2025 revenue guidance.

checks.a4: Supported so far. Two acute liver failure deaths in treated patients, following the earlier liver-enzyme signal, led to a halted trial and an independent expert review. This does not yet settle whether safety will outweigh the approvals already granted.
checks.a3: Weakened. The second death led the company to suspend its 2025 revenue guidance and pause shipments to some patients. That undercuts the assumption that revenue and cash could absorb a setback without disruption to the business itself.

updates.narrative: Sarepta paused all U.S. shipments after an FDA request, and the FDA later added a boxed warning for fatal liver injury and narrowed the approval back to ambulatory patients only, removing the 2024 non-ambulatory expansion.

checks.a1: Partly supported. Approval stands for ambulatory patients, which includes the younger subgroup, while the non-ambulatory indication was removed after fatal liver injuries in those patients. The subgroup's functional effect was never confirmed on a primary endpoint.
checks.a2: Partly supported. The FDA required a boxed warning for fatal liver injury and narrowed the label, a regulatory judgment that the risk-benefit balance had shifted for some patients. Ambulatory patients retain approval, so this is not a full withdrawal.
checks.a4: Supported so far. A boxed warning for fatal liver injury and a narrowed indication followed two deaths, a safety consequence that reached the label itself. Whether this outweighs the efficacy case over the full history is still not fully settled.

growth-005.voice: Farm and construction equipment maker reports 11% sales drop, guides both segments lower for the year, and announces layoffs with $175 million of charges.

claims.text: Q3 sales down 11%, full-year guidance down about 10% in agriculture and 25% in construction
separation programs with about $175 million of charges and $175 million of annual savings
agriculture margin expanded to 16.6% and nine-month free cash flow swung to about $3.5 billion

growth-005.question: Is a cyclical business cutting costs at the bottom, or a business in longer decline dressed up by margin discipline?

debrief_check.s1: The cutoff quarter was close to the trough: fiscal 2020 net income landed in line with guidance, fiscal 2021 was guided up and then set a record at $5.96 billion, fiscal 2022 $7.13 billion [e1][e4][e5].
debrief_check.s2: The collected record does not isolate the $175 million of savings; what it shows is profit roughly doubling within two years, with a five-week strike in late 2021 along the way [e2][e3][e4].
debrief_check.s3: The margin and cash discipline the bull side pointed to was the right tell for the trough. By year five the cycle had turned again: a record $10.2 billion in fiscal 2023, then $7.1 billion and lower guidance amid tariff costs [e7][e9][e10].

growth-005.ask_label: What would you look up before deciding?

ask_friend.q: Is this a bad quarter or a bad cycle?
ask_friend.a: Sales fell 11% to $8.9 billion and net income to $811 million, and the full year is guided to about $2.25 billion with agriculture down about 10% and construction down about 25% [c2][c3]. Yet agriculture's operating margin rose to 16.6% from 10.3% on 5% lower sales, and equipment gross margin improved to about 25.8% [c5][c10]. Management's own industry forecasts have US and Canadian large-farm equipment down 5 to 10% and it attaches 'many uncertainties' about the pandemic to its outlook [c6].

ask_friend.q: What are the layoffs worth?
ask_friend.a: Separation programmes completing in the fourth quarter carry about $175 million of pre-tax charges and are expected to save about $175 million a year [c4]. Nine-month operating cash flow was $4.1 billion against $0.4 billion a year earlier, and free cash flow about $3.5 billion, while the dividend was held at $0.76 a share [c8][c12]. Construction's operating profit fell 46% and the company is reducing dealer inventory, which can mean further production cuts [c5].

ask_friend.q: Is it expensive?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $199.50, a 12-month high, up 28% over twelve months against 16% for the market. Market capitalisation is about $63 billion, roughly 1.6 times last year's revenue of $39 billion. The company carries about $34 billion of net debt, most of it funding the captive financing arm that lends to farmers and dealers, so enterprise value overstates the industrial business [c1]. The packet has no peer multiples.

assumptions.text: This quarter is the bottom of the farm cycle.
Margin discipline will hold when volumes recover.
A stock at its 12-month high already prices the recovery.
The pandemic will keep farm and construction demand weak for years.
I don't have enough evidence to take a position either way.

thesis_check.a1: Evidence: fiscal 2020 net income landed at $2.75 billion, in line with the August guidance, and fiscal 2021 was guided up and then set a record at $5.96 billion, followed by $7.13 billion and $10.17 billion [e1][e4][e5][e7]. For this assumption: supported; the cutoff quarter was close to the trough. Unknown at the time: the crop-price upcycle that drove it, and the five-week strike in late 2021 [e2][e3].
thesis_check.a2: Evidence: profit roughly doubled within two years and tripled within three on sales growth of 24% in the first of those years [e4][e5][e7]. For this assumption: supported. Unknown: how much came from cost programmes versus pricing and mix; the record collected does not separate them.
thesis_check.a3: Evidence: the stock roughly doubled over three years; see the result tiles against SPY [e4][e5]. For this assumption: not supported; the high was not the top. Unknown: whether the same reasoning holds at the fiscal 2023 peak, after which income fell 30% and guidance dropped further [e9][e10].
thesis_check.a4: Evidence: fiscal 2021 guidance cited 'renewed optimism' from higher crop prices and the following years were records [e1][e4][e5]. For this assumption: not supported over the horizon. Unknown: the later downturn from fiscal 2024, with layoffs and tariff costs, came from a different cycle [e8][e9][e10].
thesis_check.a5: Evidence: the packet had one down quarter, a cautious forecast and strong cash flow; the decisive input was the commodity cycle, which it did not contain [e1][e4]. For this assumption: a fair reading. Unknown: whether a one-year wait would have been cheaper; the record says it would not.

walkthrough.stage_text: Three months in, the fiscal year closes with net income of $2.75 billion, in line with the August guidance. The new year is guided to $3.6 to 4.0 billion on 'renewed optimism' from higher crop prices, with agriculture sales expected up 10 to 15%.

Fourteen months in, workers at fourteen US plants walk out, the first strike at the company in thirty-five years. Production stops in the busiest year in memory; the outcome of the talks is not yet known.

Fifteen months in, with the strike settled by a six-year contract, the fiscal year sets a record: net income of $5.96 billion on 24% sales growth, more than double the year of your decision. Guidance points higher again.
Three years in, a third consecutive record, $10.2 billion of net income. In the same release the company guides the next year down, citing farm incomes and dealer inventories.

baseline.narrative: Your window ends before the first new development covered by this story: the first fiscal-year close after your entry. The starting evidence -- one down quarter, cautious full-year guidance, and margin gains -- leaves the farm-cycle question unresolved.

checks.a1: Unresolved. A single quarter's results and guidance cannot establish whether the cycle has already bottomed.
checks.a2: Unresolved. One quarter of margin improvement does not show whether discipline will hold once volumes actually recover.
checks.a3: Unresolved. The starting record does not establish how much of a future recovery a 12-month-high price already reflects.
checks.a4: Unresolved. A single down quarter and cautious guidance cannot establish how long pandemic-era weakness will persist.
checks.a5: Choosing to wait is consistent with uncertainty. This outcome alone cannot tell us whether waiting was the better decision.

updates.narrative: The fiscal year that began with the down quarter closed with net income in line with the guidance given at cutoff, and the new year was guided higher on 'renewed optimism' about crop prices.

checks.a1: Partly supported. Full-year net income landed in line with the guidance visible at cutoff, and the following year was guided up on renewed optimism about crop prices. One guidance cycle does not yet confirm the cycle has turned.
checks.a4: Weakened. The new year's guidance pointed to improving farm demand rather than continued pandemic-era weakness. A single guidance update does not settle demand over multiple years.

updates.narrative: Workers at fourteen U.S. plants went on strike in October, the company's first walkout in decades; a new six-year contract ended the five-week strike in November.

checks.a2: Unresolved. A five-week strike halted production at fourteen plants during a strong-demand stretch; the settlement's terms were not itemized in this record, so whether margin discipline held through the disruption is not yet shown.

updates.narrative: With the strike settled, the fiscal year closed at a record net income of $5.96 billion on 24% sales growth, more than double the year of the decision, and guidance pointed higher again.

checks.a1: Supported. Net income set a record, more than double the year of the decision, after the strike was settled. The cutoff quarter reads as close to the cycle's bottom.
checks.a2: Partly supported. Profit reached a record despite the strike, evidence of resilience through a demand recovery. This record does not separate cost-programme savings from pricing and mix effects.
checks.a4: Not supported. Demand accelerated to a record year rather than staying weak for years as this assumption expected. A single record year does not rule out weakness resuming later.
checks.a5: Mixed. Staying out through the record year that followed would not have been the cheaper choice on this path. That does not establish whether an even earlier or later entry would have done better.

updates.narrative: A second consecutive record followed: net income of $7.13 billion, up 19%, with guidance again pointing higher for the year ahead.

checks.a1: Supported. A second consecutive record year followed the rebound guided a year earlier. Two record years running read as confirmation of a bottom near the cutoff quarter, though one path cannot rule out coincidence.
checks.a2: Partly supported. Profit continued climbing into a second record year. This record still does not separate margin discipline from the commodity-price tailwind behind the demand.

updates.narrative: Three years in, a third consecutive record arrived: $10.2 billion in net income. In the same release, the next year was guided down, citing farm incomes and dealer inventories returning to 'mid-cycle levels.'

checks.a1: Supported. Three consecutive record years followed the cutoff quarter, consistent with a trough read at cutoff. The same release guided the next year down, a reminder this is a cycle rather than a one-way trend.
checks.a2: Supported. Profit roughly tripled within three years on the back of the first year's 24% sales growth. This record still cannot isolate cost-programme savings from pricing and mix.
checks.a3: Not supported. Over the three years since cutoff the share price roughly doubled alongside the earnings record, so the 12-month high at cutoff did not mark the top of the move. This does not establish whether the same reasoning holds at the later peak.

updates.narrative: Four years on, nearly 300 jobs were cut at Midwest plants, citing a weakening farm economy and falling orders.

checks.a4: Not supported, though later weakness had a different cause. Layoffs four years on were attributed to a weakening farm economy rather than the pandemic-era demand this assumption named at cutoff.

updates.narrative: Full-year net income fell 30% from the prior record to $7.10 billion, and the following year was guided down further to $5.0-5.5 billion amid a steep agricultural downturn.

checks.a1: Mixed. A downturn arrived four years after cutoff, well beyond the near-term bottom this assumption addressed. It does not overturn that the cutoff quarter itself read as close to a trough; cycles evidently turn more than once.
checks.a2: Weakened. Net income fell 30% from the prior record as volumes and pricing softened. This does not by itself show how much of the earlier margin gains were given back versus held.

updates.narrative: By the final data point covered here, quarterly net income was down 26% year over year, with tariff costs near $200 million cited alongside the decline, and shares fell in premarket trading on the report.

checks.a1: Mixed. Quarterly income fell 26% with tariff costs cited, extending the downturn from the prior update. This does not overturn that the cutoff quarter was close to a bottom within its own multi-year cycle.
checks.a2: Weakened further. Tariff costs and falling income continued the pattern from the prior year's downturn. This record still cannot separate cost discipline from cyclical and trade pressures.

growth-004.voice: One analyst: the retailer just added $15 billion of sales in a year, took $9 billion of share, and lifted returns on capital to 23%; the pandemic changed its position for good. The other: it refuses to guide, two-thirds of the growth was digital at 145%, and digital fulfilment already costs gross margin.

claims.text: FY2020 comparable sales up 19.3%, about $9 billion of share gained, ROIC 23.5%
no FY2021 sales or EPS guidance, citing uncertainty
digital fulfilment and supply-chain costs already weighing on gross margin

growth-004.question: Which assumption explains the split: durable share gain, or a one-off year the company itself won't extrapolate?

debrief_check.s1: Held for exactly one more year: fiscal 2021 comparable sales rose a further 12.7% and adjusted EPS 44% [e1]. Then fiscal 2022 operating income fell 57% as the company worked through inventory, and comparable sales turned negative in 2023 [e2][e4][e5][e6].
debrief_check.s2: Guidance resumed a year later, and that guidance was cut twice within months [e1][e2][e3]. The refusal to guide was an honest signal of unpredictability, not a bluff.
debrief_check.s3: Costs did crush margin in 2022, though the trigger was excess inventory in discretionary categories rather than digital fulfilment itself [e2][e4]. The second analyst's assumption, that the year was not repeatable, was the one that explained the split.

growth-004.ask_label: What would you ask the two analysts?

ask_friend.q: How much of the growth was the pandemic year?
ask_friend.a: Fiscal 2020 added more than $15 billion of sales, more than the previous eleven years of growth combined, with comparable sales up 19.3% and digital comparable sales up 145% [c8][c2]. Digital was about two-thirds of the fourth quarter's growth [c12]. The company says it gained about $9 billion of market share across all five core categories [c9]; it does not say how much of the year's volume it expects to keep.

ask_friend.q: Why won't the company guide?
ask_friend.a: Management said continued COVID-19 uncertainty is the reason it gives no fiscal 2021 sales or EPS guidance [c3][c6][c11]. What it did disclose: operating margin rose to 7.0% from 6.0%, after-tax return on invested capital to 23.5% from 16.0%, cash of $8.5 billion, and a resumed buyback with about $4.5 billion of capacity [c4][c10][c5]. It also said digital fulfilment and supply-chain costs already weigh on gross margin [c14], and the current portion of long-term debt rose to $1.1 billion [c13].

ask_friend.q: Is it expensive?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $173.49, up 59% over twelve months against 25% for the market, 13% below the 12-month high. The cash pile and new CEO will buy or build a second growth engine.
A 3x revenue multiple with $31 billion of cash is already a floor.
Generic erosion will spread from hepatitis C to HIV within five years.
My friend is right: shrinking revenue and a written-off bet make this a trap.

thesis_check.a1: Evidence: HIV revenue rose to $16.4 billion in 2019 while hepatitis C fell to $2.9 billion; the lead regimen passed $10 billion by 2022 and a twice-yearly injectable was approved [e2][e8][e9]. For this assumption: supported throughout. Unknown at the cutoff: a pandemic antiviral that added a large revenue line for two years [e5][e6].
thesis_check.a2: Evidence: the new CEO bought Immunomedics for $21 billion in September 2020 to add an oncology drug, later approved in a much larger breast-cancer population [e1][e3][e7][e10]. For this assumption: supported in form. Unknown: whether the price paid earns a return; revenue was flat at $27.3 billion in 2022 [e9].
thesis_check.a3: Evidence: the shares rose over five years but lagged the market by a wide margin; see the result tiles. For this assumption: a floor, not a spring. Unknown: how much the pandemic drug distorted the middle years.
thesis_check.a4: Evidence: an older HIV drug lost US exclusivity a year early in 2020 [e4], yet HIV revenue kept growing on the newer regimen [e2][e9]. For this assumption: partly right on the event, wrong on the effect. Unknown: the next patent cliff, outside this window.
thesis_check.a5: Evidence: revenue did not shrink further; it grew to $27.3 billion, with new products and two acquisitions [e3][e9][e10]. For this assumption: not a trap in the sense of a shrinking business; the friend's fear about the return relative to the market was closer to the mark. Unknown: what the shares would have done without the pandemic drug's two strong years.

walkthrough.stage_text: Three weeks in, the new chief executive, from a large European pharma, takes over as planned. No strategy is announced yet.

One year in, full-year 2019 revenue is $22.4 billion: HIV up to $16.4 billion on the new regimen, hepatitis C down to $2.9 billion. The pattern the packet described has continued, and the total is flat.

Nineteen months in, the company agrees to buy Immunomedics for about $21 billion in cash for a breast-cancer drug approved five months earlier. A month later, a generic of an older HIV drug launches a year sooner than expected, and its antiviral is approved as the first treatment for the pandemic virus.

Four years in, 2022 revenue is flat at $27.3 billion: the lead HIV regimen passes $10 billion, the pandemic antiviral falls 30%, and the acquired cancer drug is a day from approval in a common form of breast cancer.
